We understand the desire to take corporate money out of elections.
This year’s race for California governor (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/california-governor-contributions-takeaways/) highlights that need more than ever. A political spending committee comprising the state realtors association, California Chamber of Commerce, Pacific Gas & Electric and the state electrical workers union spent a record $32 million on ads opposing Democratic billionaire Tom Steyer, who ultimately placed third in the primary.
Leading into those primaries, Democratic nominee Xavier Becerra — whose name appears on the Nov. 3 ballot — was backed by Meta, AirBnB and Uber at $1 million each and Chevron, McDonalds and DaVita at $500,000 each, to name a few.
Those corporate dollars force the fair question: If elected, how confident are we that Becerra will have the people’s interests at heart, and not those corporations’?
Not solution
Many counties are already struggling financially. Some have placed sales tax measures on the ballot this year to bring more revenue into their general funds. Some already had sales tax measures on the ballot in 2024. And some still face a budget deficit. Other counties may be sitting on the fence, but there is no wiggle room in their budgets to create a fund for campaign financing.
Moreover, people should be able to decide if they want their money to go toward supporting a candidate. Our elected officials should not make that decision for us — especially if they are up for re-election.
We agree that special interests should not be able to buy candidates or campaigns, but Proposition 4 is not the answer. Creating a fund of taxpayer dollars and making it available for election campaigns is not the answer. Those hard-earned dollars belong in a municipality’s general fund, to be used on improving roadways, funding for public safety officers or enhancing our local parks.
Reject Proposition 4.

There is little evidence in California and across the nation that public financing of candidates has had the broadly beneficial effects that advocates predicted. (SCNG)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 4, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: September 10, 2026 at 10:32 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Few political beliefs are as fervently held as the view that public financing of candidates would quickly improve their quality and variety, reduce the clout of “special interests,” and promote both public trust and better government.
This is why Californians will be asked in November to enact Proposition 4 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_4,_Allow_Public_Financing_of_Election_Campaigns_Measure_(2026)), which would overturn the voter-approved 1988 law that prohibits state and local governments from using taxpayer money to provide campaign funding to candidates.
The state Legislature placed the measure on the ballot after being urged to do so (https://laist.com/news/politics/public-funding-for-elections-the-idea-is-back-in-california-fair-elections-act-ben-allen) by groups such as the League of Women Voters, which argues that public financing “helps engage unrepresented communities in the political process” and “makes our democracy ultimately much stronger.”
But most claims made by advocates don’t hold up. There is no empirical evidence that shows public financing of candidates improves governance.
In California, charter cities are allowed to provide public financing. All five that have done so — Los Angeles, Long Beach, San Francisco, Oakland and Berkeley — are considered poorly run. They’re dominated by government unions, by far the Golden State’s most powerful special interest.
Meanwhile, most of the 14 states that allow for public financing have programs that are little-used or practically defunct. Those with higher participation (such as Arizona, Minnesota and New York) usually show modest increases (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/state-politics-and-policy-quarterly/article/does-public-financing-motivate-electoral-challengers/6365D1FA24C0A905E69A899B678909C5) in candidate diversity. They also undercut claims that public financing will lead to a flood of unqualified candidates who are eager to use taxpayer funds to spread their views.
But whether in California or these states, there is no evidence that public financing has led to different policy outcomes or increased public trust.
Defenders of the reform will say that’s because there’s so much private financing — i.e., special interest money — in elections. But that’s not going to change. The Supreme Court has repeatedly made clear that paid political speech is constitutionally protected free speech.
So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits. Even if California wasn’t in an era of tight local and state budgets, this measure would deserve to be rejected.
The final paragraph has been revised to more precisely describe Proposition 4's effects if approved. It would not automatically require more government spending. State and local lawmakers would need to approve public financing of candidate campaigns for that to happen.

There is little evidence in California and across the nation that public financing of candidates has had the broadly beneficial effects that advocates predicted. (SCNG)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 4, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: September 10, 2026 at 10:32 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Few political beliefs are as fervently held as the view that public financing of candidates would quickly improve their quality and variety, reduce the clout of “special interests,” and promote both public trust and better government.
This is why Californians will be asked in November to enact Proposition 4 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_4,_Allow_Public_Financing_of_Election_Campaigns_Measure_(2026)), which would overturn the voter-approved 1988 law that prohibits state and local governments from using taxpayer money to provide campaign funding to candidates.
The state Legislature placed the measure on the ballot after being urged to do so (https://laist.com/news/politics/public-funding-for-elections-the-idea-is-back-in-california-fair-elections-act-ben-allen) by groups such as the League of Women Voters, which argues that public financing “helps engage unrepresented communities in the political process” and “makes our democracy ultimately much stronger.”
But most claims made by advocates don’t hold up. There is no empirical evidence that shows public financing of candidates improves governance.
In California, charter cities are allowed to provide public financing. All five that have done so — Los Angeles, Long Beach, San Francisco, Oakland and Berkeley — are considered poorly run. They’re dominated by government unions, by far the Golden State’s most powerful special interest.
Meanwhile, most of the 14 states that allow for public financing have programs that are little-used or practically defunct. Those with higher participation (such as Arizona, Minnesota and New York) usually show modest increases (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/state-politics-and-policy-quarterly/article/does-public-financing-motivate-electoral-challengers/6365D1FA24C0A905E69A899B678909C5) in candidate diversity. They also undercut claims that public financing will lead to a flood of unqualified candidates who are eager to use taxpayer funds to spread their views.
But whether in California or these states, there is no evidence that public financing has led to different policy outcomes or increased public trust.
Defenders of the reform will say that’s because there’s so much private financing — i.e., special interest money — in elections. But that’s not going to change. The Supreme Court has repeatedly made clear that paid political speech is constitutionally protected free speech.
So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits. Even if California wasn’t in an era of tight local and state budgets, this measure would deserve to be rejected.
The final paragraph has been revised to more precisely describe Proposition 4's effects if approved. It would not automatically require more government spending. State and local lawmakers would need to approve public financing of candidate campaigns for that to happen.

Good — I now have the actual text. Key provisions:
- Amends Gov Code 85300: a public officer shall not expend, and a candidate shall not accept, public funds for seeking elective office IF the funds are earmarked by a state/local entity for education, transportation, or public safety. So the absolute ban becomes conditional.
- Candidates must abide by expenditure limits and meet strict criteria (defined: demonstrate broad-based support, e.g., small-dollar contributions capped at $10 counted; can't require signatures or raising a total dollar amount more than $10 per contributor).
- Public funds can't pay legal defense fees or fines.
- Can't repay personal loans with public funds; and if you receive public funds, can't repay personal loans with any funds after campaign ends.
- Public funding must be available to all qualified, voluntarily participating candidates without regard to incumbency or party preference; no discrimination based on party or incumbent/challenger status.
- Expenditure limits can be increased by formula tied to net supportive funds of opponents.
- FPPC not responsible for administration/enforcement of local public funding systems.
- Triples fines for foreign contributions (from 1x to up to 3x).

So opponents' claims: "no limit on the number of candidates," "no limit on how much money" — partly true in the sense the measure doesn't set dollar amounts; it requires expenditure limits be set by each jurisdiction. The rebuttal: Prop 4 requires expenditure limits and strict criteria; amounts are left to local governments. Also note: "It even allows for public financing of candidates for county political party committees" — need to check. The Political Reform Act's definition of "candidate" includes candidates for county central committee? Let me check. Actually Gov Code 82011 defines "candidate" as an individual seeking elective office... hmm. Let me verify.

Also, "they don't even have to actually qualify for the ballot to get taxpayer money" — the strict criteria require broad-based support but not signature thresholds. That's a real point: Prop 4 prohibits requiring signatures, which is a notable drafting choice. Critics say that means candidates who never make the ballot could get public funds.

The influence of money on political races has gotten out of control, but allowing candidates to accept public funds — taxpayer dollars — for campaign purposes is not the answer.
We recommend voting “no” on Proposition 4. Our tax dollars should not be spent on election campaigns.
Related Articles
Endorsement: Break the 49ers’ grip over Santa Clara. Elect these three candidates. (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/31/endorsement-break-the-49ers-grip-over-santa-clara-make-kertes-mayor-elect-inciarte-and-crutchlow-to-council/)
Endorsement: These three City Council candidates are San Jose’s best choices (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-peter-ortiz-bien-doan-and-genny-altwer-to-san-jose-city-council/)
Endorsement: Elect Michael Melillo to San Jose Unified School District Board of Education (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-michael-melillo-to-san-jose-unified-school-district-board-of-education/)
Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)
Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
Sky-high spending
Consider this news organization’s report last week (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/11/whos-donating-to-the-billionaire-backed-group-has-raised-almost-300-million-to-fight-the-wealth-tax/) showing how a single political action committee backed by billionaires — Building a Better California — has spent nearly a quarter of a billion dollars this year alone, breaking all previous records.
Understandably alarmed, this inundation of money into state politics has pushed legislators to ask voters this November to repeal a 1988 law and allow taxpayer dollars to be spent on campaigns.
A “yes” vote would allow state and local governments to create programs so that public funds — again, taxpayer dollars — could be set aside for election campaigns.
We understand the desire to take corporate money out of elections.
This year’s race for California governor (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/california-governor-contributions-takeaways/) highlights that need more than ever. A political spending committee comprising the state realtors association, California Chamber of Commerce, Pacific Gas & Electric and the state electrical workers union spent a record $32 million on ads opposing Democratic billionaire Tom Steyer, who ultimately placed third in the primary.
Leading into those primaries, Democratic nominee Xavier Becerra — whose name appears on the Nov. 3 ballot — was backed by Meta, AirBnB and Uber at $1 million each and Chevron, McDonalds and DaVita at $500,000 each, to name a few.
Those corporate dollars force the fair question: If elected, how confident are we that Becerra will have the people’s interests at heart, and not those corporations’?
Not solution
Many counties are already struggling financially. Some have placed sales tax measures on the ballot this year to bring more revenue into their general funds. Some already had sales tax measures on the ballot in 2024. And some still face a budget deficit. Other counties may be sitting on the fence, but there is no wiggle room in their budgets to create a fund for campaign financing.
Moreover, people should be able to decide if they want their money to go toward supporting a candidate. Our elected officials should not make that decision for us — especially if they are up for re-election.
We agree that special interests should not be able to buy candidates or campaigns, but Proposition 4 is not the answer. Creating a fund of taxpayer dollars and making it available for election campaigns is not the answer. Those hard-earned dollars belong in a municipality’s general fund, to be used on improving roadways, funding for public safety officers or enhancing our local parks.
Reject Proposition 4.

There is little evidence in California and across the nation that public financing of candidates has had the broadly beneficial effects that advocates predicted. (SCNG)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 4, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: September 10, 2026 at 10:32 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Few political beliefs are as fervently held as the view that public financing of candidates would quickly improve their quality and variety, reduce the clout of “special interests,” and promote both public trust and better government.
This is why Californians will be asked in November to enact Proposition 4 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_4,_Allow_Public_Financing_of_Election_Campaigns_Measure_(2026)), which would overturn the voter-approved 1988 law that prohibits state and local governments from using taxpayer money to provide campaign funding to candidates.
The state Legislature placed the measure on the ballot after being urged to do so (https://laist.com/news/politics/public-funding-for-elections-the-idea-is-back-in-california-fair-elections-act-ben-allen) by groups such as the League of Women Voters, which argues that public financing “helps engage unrepresented communities in the political process” and “makes our democracy ultimately much stronger.”
But most claims made by advocates don’t hold up. There is no empirical evidence that shows public financing of candidates improves governance.
In California, charter cities are allowed to provide public financing. All five that have done so — Los Angeles, Long Beach, San Francisco, Oakland and Berkeley — are considered poorly run. They’re dominated by government unions, by far the Golden State’s most powerful special interest.
Meanwhile, most of the 14 states that allow for public financing have programs that are little-used or practically defunct. Those with higher participation (such as Arizona, Minnesota and New York) usually show modest increases (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/state-politics-and-policy-quarterly/article/does-public-financing-motivate-electoral-challengers/6365D1FA24C0A905E69A899B678909C5) in candidate diversity. They also undercut claims that public financing will lead to a flood of unqualified candidates who are eager to use taxpayer funds to spread their views.
But whether in California or these states, there is no evidence that public financing has led to different policy outcomes or increased public trust.
Defenders of the reform will say that’s because there’s so much private financing — i.e., special interest money — in elections. But that’s not going to change. The Supreme Court has repeatedly made clear that paid political speech is constitutionally protected free speech.
So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits. Even if California wasn’t in an era of tight local and state budgets, this measure would deserve to be rejected.
The final paragraph has been revised to more precisely describe Proposition 4's effects if approved. It would not automatically require more government spending. State and local lawmakers would need to approve public financing of candidate campaigns for that to happen.

How to vote on California’s Proposition 4: McClatchy Media’s recommendation | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 2, 2026 4:49 PM
"I voted" stickers await voters at the Placer County Clerk-Recorder-Elections Office in Rocklin on Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. Proposition 4 would repeal California’s ban on public financing of political campaigns.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Of the 14 propositions on California’s November ballot, Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html) could be one of the least accessible to the average voter.
Here is what you need to know: A “Yes” vote on Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on the use of tax dollars to fund local and state elections.
“The measure (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=4&year=2026) would allow state and local governments to create programs for the use of certain public funds to finance political campaigns,” wrote The Bee last week. “Candidates would be prohibited from using the funds to repay personal loans to their campaigns, legal defense fees or fines. Those who receive public funds would be required to show broad-based local support and pledge their compliance with spending limits and other rules.”
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html)
Public money set aside for education, transportation or public safety would not be available to be used for local and state elections. “Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate’s personal campaign loan,” wrote the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
“We just want to lift the ban, putting into place certain reasonable, common-sense taxpayer requirements so that communities have the opportunity to use public financing to allow qualified candidates the chance to run,” said Trent Lange, president and executive director of the California Clean Money Campaign.
Other groups in favor of Prop. 4 include the California Democratic Party, ACLU California Action (https://aclucalaction.org/2026-election-guide/), California Clean Money Action Fund, End Citizens United and the League of Women Voters of California, as well as state senators Ben Allen, D-Santa Monica; Sabrina Cervantes, D-Riverside; and Tom Umberg, D-Villa Park. Those in opposition are the California Republican Party, Reform California and California Taxpayers Association.
The editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/)Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) recommend a “Yes” vote on Prop. 4. The measure would end the state’s overly restrictive ban on public financing of campaigns. Public financing amplifies the voices of everyday voters and gives candidates an alternative to relying on wealthy donors.
A “Yes” vote would allow local governments to create matching-fund programs, in which public money matches small private donations, or public campaign-grant programs that provide qualifying candidates with a set amount of taxpayer money. Such programs would reduce candidates’ dependence on large donors and political committees, lower barriers to running for office, and help build a more diverse and representative democracy.
“Everybody knows that the amount of money in politics is outrageous, and it’s corrupting our democracy,” Lange told the board.
“All that money buys access for special interests while shutting out the rest of us. We believe that we need to change the way we finance election campaigns so that elected officials can focus on working for the people, rather than their big-money donors.”

## Proposition 4 trails 42% to 53% in PPIC polling with Newsom and Democrats in support:
PPIC's September survey of likely voters, fielded September 4–10, found 42% yes, 53% no and 5% undecided, making Prop 4 one of the weakest measures on the ballot.
Republicans oppose it 78% to 19% and independents 54% to 41%, while Democrats support it 55% to 39%.
Self-described liberals back it 62% to 34%.
Renters split 50% yes to 48% no while homeowners oppose it 55% to 39%, and households earning under $40,000 lean yes, 50% to 46%.
One percent of likely voters named it the measure they are most interested in.
UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies, polling September 15–20, found 35% yes and 35% no with the rest undecided.
PPIC's October survey had not been released as of October 18.

How to vote on California’s Proposition 4: McClatchy Media’s recommendation | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 2, 2026 4:49 PM
"I voted" stickers await voters at the Placer County Clerk-Recorder-Elections Office in Rocklin on Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. Proposition 4 would repeal California’s ban on public financing of political campaigns.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Of the 14 propositions on California’s November ballot, Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html) could be one of the least accessible to the average voter.
Here is what you need to know: A “Yes” vote on Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on the use of tax dollars to fund local and state elections.
“The measure (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=4&year=2026) would allow state and local governments to create programs for the use of certain public funds to finance political campaigns,” wrote The Bee last week. “Candidates would be prohibited from using the funds to repay personal loans to their campaigns, legal defense fees or fines. Those who receive public funds would be required to show broad-based local support and pledge their compliance with spending limits and other rules.”
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html)
Public money set aside for education, transportation or public safety would not be available to be used for local and state elections. “Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate’s personal campaign loan,” wrote the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
“We just want to lift the ban, putting into place certain reasonable, common-sense taxpayer requirements so that communities have the opportunity to use public financing to allow qualified candidates the chance to run,” said Trent Lange, president and executive director of the California Clean Money Campaign.
Other groups in favor of Prop. 4 include the California Democratic Party, ACLU California Action (https://aclucalaction.org/2026-election-guide/), California Clean Money Action Fund, End Citizens United and the League of Women Voters of California, as well as state senators Ben Allen, D-Santa Monica; Sabrina Cervantes, D-Riverside; and Tom Umberg, D-Villa Park. Those in opposition are the California Republican Party, Reform California and California Taxpayers Association.
The editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/)Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) recommend a “Yes” vote on Prop. 4. The measure would end the state’s overly restrictive ban on public financing of campaigns. Public financing amplifies the voices of everyday voters and gives candidates an alternative to relying on wealthy donors.
A “Yes” vote would allow local governments to create matching-fund programs, in which public money matches small private donations, or public campaign-grant programs that provide qualifying candidates with a set amount of taxpayer money. Such programs would reduce candidates’ dependence on large donors and political committees, lower barriers to running for office, and help build a more diverse and representative democracy.
“Everybody knows that the amount of money in politics is outrageous, and it’s corrupting our democracy,” Lange told the board.
“All that money buys access for special interests while shutting out the rest of us. We believe that we need to change the way we finance election campaigns so that elected officials can focus on working for the people, rather than their big-money donors.”

How to vote on California’s Proposition 4: McClatchy Media’s recommendation | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 2, 2026 4:49 PM
"I voted" stickers await voters at the Placer County Clerk-Recorder-Elections Office in Rocklin on Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. Proposition 4 would repeal California’s ban on public financing of political campaigns.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Of the 14 propositions on California’s November ballot, Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html) could be one of the least accessible to the average voter.
Here is what you need to know: A “Yes” vote on Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on the use of tax dollars to fund local and state elections.
“The measure (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=4&year=2026) would allow state and local governments to create programs for the use of certain public funds to finance political campaigns,” wrote The Bee last week. “Candidates would be prohibited from using the funds to repay personal loans to their campaigns, legal defense fees or fines. Those who receive public funds would be required to show broad-based local support and pledge their compliance with spending limits and other rules.”
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html)
Public money set aside for education, transportation or public safety would not be available to be used for local and state elections. “Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate’s personal campaign loan,” wrote the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
“We just want to lift the ban, putting into place certain reasonable, common-sense taxpayer requirements so that communities have the opportunity to use public financing to allow qualified candidates the chance to run,” said Trent Lange, president and executive director of the California Clean Money Campaign.
Other groups in favor of Prop. 4 include the California Democratic Party, ACLU California Action (https://aclucalaction.org/2026-election-guide/), California Clean Money Action Fund, End Citizens United and the League of Women Voters of California, as well as state senators Ben Allen, D-Santa Monica; Sabrina Cervantes, D-Riverside; and Tom Umberg, D-Villa Park. Those in opposition are the California Republican Party, Reform California and California Taxpayers Association.
The editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/)Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) recommend a “Yes” vote on Prop. 4. The measure would end the state’s overly restrictive ban on public financing of campaigns. Public financing amplifies the voices of everyday voters and gives candidates an alternative to relying on wealthy donors.
A “Yes” vote would allow local governments to create matching-fund programs, in which public money matches small private donations, or public campaign-grant programs that provide qualifying candidates with a set amount of taxpayer money. Such programs would reduce candidates’ dependence on large donors and political committees, lower barriers to running for office, and help build a more diverse and representative democracy.
“Everybody knows that the amount of money in politics is outrageous, and it’s corrupting our democracy,” Lange told the board.
“All that money buys access for special interests while shutting out the rest of us. We believe that we need to change the way we finance election campaigns so that elected officials can focus on working for the people, rather than their big-money donors.”

## Proposition 4 trails 42% to 53% in PPIC polling with Newsom and Democrats in support:
PPIC's September survey of likely voters, fielded September 4–10, found 42% yes, 53% no and 5% undecided, making Prop 4 one of the weakest measures on the ballot.
Republicans oppose it 78% to 19% and independents 54% to 41%, while Democrats support it 55% to 39%.
Self-described liberals back it 62% to 34%.
Renters split 50% yes to 48% no while homeowners oppose it 55% to 39%, and households earning under $40,000 lean yes, 50% to 46%.
One percent of likely voters named it the measure they are most interested in.
UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies, polling September 15–20, found 35% yes and 35% no with the rest undecided.
PPIC's October survey had not been released as of October 18.

How to vote on California’s Proposition 4: McClatchy Media’s recommendation | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 2, 2026 4:49 PM
"I voted" stickers await voters at the Placer County Clerk-Recorder-Elections Office in Rocklin on Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. Proposition 4 would repeal California’s ban on public financing of political campaigns.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Of the 14 propositions on California’s November ballot, Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html) could be one of the least accessible to the average voter.
Here is what you need to know: A “Yes” vote on Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on the use of tax dollars to fund local and state elections.
“The measure (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=4&year=2026) would allow state and local governments to create programs for the use of certain public funds to finance political campaigns,” wrote The Bee last week. “Candidates would be prohibited from using the funds to repay personal loans to their campaigns, legal defense fees or fines. Those who receive public funds would be required to show broad-based local support and pledge their compliance with spending limits and other rules.”
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html)
Public money set aside for education, transportation or public safety would not be available to be used for local and state elections. “Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate’s personal campaign loan,” wrote the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
“We just want to lift the ban, putting into place certain reasonable, common-sense taxpayer requirements so that communities have the opportunity to use public financing to allow qualified candidates the chance to run,” said Trent Lange, president and executive director of the California Clean Money Campaign.
Other groups in favor of Prop. 4 include the California Democratic Party, ACLU California Action (https://aclucalaction.org/2026-election-guide/), California Clean Money Action Fund, End Citizens United and the League of Women Voters of California, as well as state senators Ben Allen, D-Santa Monica; Sabrina Cervantes, D-Riverside; and Tom Umberg, D-Villa Park. Those in opposition are the California Republican Party, Reform California and California Taxpayers Association.
The editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/)Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) recommend a “Yes” vote on Prop. 4. The measure would end the state’s overly restrictive ban on public financing of campaigns. Public financing amplifies the voices of everyday voters and gives candidates an alternative to relying on wealthy donors.
A “Yes” vote would allow local governments to create matching-fund programs, in which public money matches small private donations, or public campaign-grant programs that provide qualifying candidates with a set amount of taxpayer money. Such programs would reduce candidates’ dependence on large donors and political committees, lower barriers to running for office, and help build a more diverse and representative democracy.
“Everybody knows that the amount of money in politics is outrageous, and it’s corrupting our democracy,” Lange told the board.
“All that money buys access for special interests while shutting out the rest of us. We believe that we need to change the way we finance election campaigns so that elected officials can focus on working for the people, rather than their big-money donors.”

## Proposition 4 trails 42% to 53% in PPIC polling with Newsom and Democrats in support:
PPIC's September survey of likely voters, fielded September 4–10, found 42% yes, 53% no and 5% undecided, making Prop 4 one of the weakest measures on the ballot.
Republicans oppose it 78% to 19% and independents 54% to 41%, while Democrats support it 55% to 39%.
Self-described liberals back it 62% to 34%.
Renters split 50% yes to 48% no while homeowners oppose it 55% to 39%, and households earning under $40,000 lean yes, 50% to 46%.
One percent of likely voters named it the measure they are most interested in.
UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies, polling September 15–20, found 35% yes and 35% no with the rest undecided.
PPIC's October survey had not been released as of October 18.

A group of legislators is seeking to lift the ban on public financing for elections in California, a move to counter the ever-increasing amount of money spent on campaigns in the Golden State.
Supporters say the California Fair Elections Act could be a game changer for underfunded candidates facing well-financed opponents and make races more competitive.
“The California Fair Elections Act is all about trying to improve our Democracy and elections,” said Sen. Ben Allen (D-Santa Monica), who co-authored the bill, in a statement to LAist. “Public financing programs serve as a tool to lessen the power of big money, expand opportunities for more people to run for office, and allow candidates to focus more on voter appeal instead of donor appeal.”
If passed, SB42, would place the measure on the November 2026 ballot. Sen. Tom Umberg (D-Anaheim) and Sen. Sabrina Cervantes (D-Riverside) are sponsors.
Common Cause, a group that fights to strengthen democracy, is among the bill’s backers.
“It’s essentially leveling the playing field,” said Sean McMorris, the group’s transparency, ethics and accountability program manager. “It’s also an attempt to diversify the candidate field, which gives voters more choice.”
Opponents of the bill, including the California Taxpayers Association, say public money should not be given to people running for office — that the money is better spent on services for the public.
Sponsored message
Right now, only cities governed by their own charter may enact public financing. And five of the state's 121 charter cities, including Los Angeles, Long Beach, San Francisco, Oakland and Berkeley, have done that.
Under the proposed ballot measure, the state’s other 361 cities and 58 counties would be able to set up public financing in their jurisdictions. In addition, the state Legislature could establish public financing for statewide offices, the senate and the assembly.
The measure would allow a candidate to accept public funds unless the funds are earmarked by a state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety.
The bill would also require candidates to abide by expenditure limits and prohibit public funds from being used to pay legal defense fees, fines or to repay personal loans to their campaign.
Ways to publicly finance campaigns
There are a variety of public campaign financing schemes where governments use taxpayer money to fund candidates who agree to limit their spending.
In Los Angeles, candidates for City Council who agree to spending limits must first raise $5 each from 100 residents in their respective districts and about $77,000 from residents anywhere in the city before they qualify for matching funds.
Sponsored message
In the last election cycle, the maximum matching funds for the primary and general elections combined was $425,000. The city doled out $3.8 million in matching funds.
Trent Lange of the California Clean Money Campaign, which backs the bill, said public financing has helped diversify the L.A. City Council, which has gone from one woman member a decade ago to eight now.
“All of them were elected using public funds that helped them get their message out and run and compete,” Lange told LAist.
In the 2022 L.A. mayor’s race, billionaire Rick Caruso spent more than $100 million compared to Mayor Karen Bass’ roughly $10 million. But Bass benefitted from $2.3 million in matching funds.
Caruso rejected spending limits, which prohibited him from receiving matching funds.
In Oakland, voters have approved a voucher program. Under the program, the city will disperse $100 in so-called Democracy Dollar vouchers to eligible residents who can then give the money to the candidate of their choice. Eligible residents must be 18-years-old, an Oakland resident and a U.S. resident or green card holder.
The program, which puts free cash in the hands of voters to spend on campaigns, launches in 2026.
Sponsored message
A group called Los Angeles for Democracy Vouchers is lobbying L.A. to institute democracy vouchers.
Previous efforts have failed
Lange said two other efforts to overturn the statewide ban on public financing failed in 2006 and 2010.
That was before the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2010 landmark Citizens United decision, which prohibited restrictions on expenditures in politics.
“That decision really, really exploded the amount of money spent in politics and really raised the understanding that voters have about the problems of big money in politics,” Lange said.
Opponents of public financing of elections argue it diverts public money from more pressing needs. Republicans have generally opposed using taxpayer dollars to finance political campaigns.
“People when they pay taxes want to pay for schools, fire departments, libraries, roads, that sort of thing,” David Kline of the California Taxpayers Association said. “The last thing they want to pay for is a negative political ad that is going to hit them on the radio or T.V. during election season.”
Sponsored message
He noted someone you disagree with is going to end up getting your tax dollars under public financing of campaigns.
UCLA Law Professor Rick Hasen, director of the school’s Safeguarding Democracy Project, called public financing of elections “potentially democratizing.”
“Some of the systems have allowed for more non-traditional candidates to run - more women and racial minorities for example,” he said.
But some worry that empowering small dollar donors with matching funds can fuel more extreme candidates, Hasen said, noting those candidates can attract large numbers of small donors.
“If you give matching funds, you might be fueling that tendency to reward flashier or more extreme candidates,” he said.
Hasen noted public financing does nothing to prevent exorbitant spending by outside groups like labor unions, corporations and wealthy individuals on campaigns.
Nonetheless, Dora Rose, of the League of Women Voters, said public financing has been a top priority of the organization.
“Public financing really helps engage unrepresented communities in the political process and it makes our democracy ultimately much stronger,” she said.
Incumbents may balk
It's far from clear that the Democrat dominated state Legislature will place the measure on the ballot.
Politicians elected under one system tend to like that system, said Fredric Woocher, an attorney and recognized expert on campaign finance law.
“Obviously, under the current system it's easier to raise funds as an incumbent than it is as a challenger,” he told LAist.
Woocher said, progressive candidates in Los Angeles who otherwise may have been underfunded have benefitted from public financing.
“We’ve seen a number of these progressive candidates compete in elections and win in races where they probably wouldn’t have been able to without public financing,” he said.
Woocher pointed to the victory of progressive candidate Zohran Mamdani in New York’s Democratic primary for mayor as another example of matching funds helping a progressive candidate.
Umberg, one of the sponsors of the bill, said if the Legislature places the measure on the ballot and voters approve it, voters in individual cities would still need to approve public financing. “Its not mandatory,” he said.
“The playing field is never going to be completely level but it is a step toward leveling the playing field where the average Joe or Jane has a more profound voice than they do today,” Umberg said.
The bill is currently being held in the Assembly Appropriations Committee. A vote is expected on Aug. 29.
If approved, it would move to the full Assembly.

The measure would allow any state or local government to set up a public financing program for election campaigns.
Candidates would need to meet certain eligibility criteria and agree to spending limits.
The funds could not be used for legal defense costs, fines or repayment of personal loans.
Proposition 4 would repeal a 1988 ban on using taxpayer dollars for election campaigns.
Currently, only charter cities and counties can bypass that ban.

A group of legislators is seeking to lift the ban on public financing for elections in California, a move to counter the ever-increasing amount of money spent on campaigns in the Golden State.
Supporters say the California Fair Elections Act could be a game changer for underfunded candidates facing well-financed opponents and make races more competitive.
“The California Fair Elections Act is all about trying to improve our Democracy and elections,” said Sen. Ben Allen (D-Santa Monica), who co-authored the bill, in a statement to LAist. “Public financing programs serve as a tool to lessen the power of big money, expand opportunities for more people to run for office, and allow candidates to focus more on voter appeal instead of donor appeal.”
If passed, SB42, would place the measure on the November 2026 ballot. Sen. Tom Umberg (D-Anaheim) and Sen. Sabrina Cervantes (D-Riverside) are sponsors.
Common Cause, a group that fights to strengthen democracy, is among the bill’s backers.
“It’s essentially leveling the playing field,” said Sean McMorris, the group’s transparency, ethics and accountability program manager. “It’s also an attempt to diversify the candidate field, which gives voters more choice.”
Opponents of the bill, including the California Taxpayers Association, say public money should not be given to people running for office — that the money is better spent on services for the public.
Sponsored message
Right now, only cities governed by their own charter may enact public financing. And five of the state's 121 charter cities, including Los Angeles, Long Beach, San Francisco, Oakland and Berkeley, have done that.
Under the proposed ballot measure, the state’s other 361 cities and 58 counties would be able to set up public financing in their jurisdictions. In addition, the state Legislature could establish public financing for statewide offices, the senate and the assembly.
The measure would allow a candidate to accept public funds unless the funds are earmarked by a state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety.
The bill would also require candidates to abide by expenditure limits and prohibit public funds from being used to pay legal defense fees, fines or to repay personal loans to their campaign.
Ways to publicly finance campaigns
There are a variety of public campaign financing schemes where governments use taxpayer money to fund candidates who agree to limit their spending.
In Los Angeles, candidates for City Council who agree to spending limits must first raise $5 each from 100 residents in their respective districts and about $77,000 from residents anywhere in the city before they qualify for matching funds.
Sponsored message
In the last election cycle, the maximum matching funds for the primary and general elections combined was $425,000. The city doled out $3.8 million in matching funds.
Trent Lange of the California Clean Money Campaign, which backs the bill, said public financing has helped diversify the L.A. City Council, which has gone from one woman member a decade ago to eight now.
“All of them were elected using public funds that helped them get their message out and run and compete,” Lange told LAist.
In the 2022 L.A. mayor’s race, billionaire Rick Caruso spent more than $100 million compared to Mayor Karen Bass’ roughly $10 million. But Bass benefitted from $2.3 million in matching funds.
Caruso rejected spending limits, which prohibited him from receiving matching funds.
In Oakland, voters have approved a voucher program. Under the program, the city will disperse $100 in so-called Democracy Dollar vouchers to eligible residents who can then give the money to the candidate of their choice. Eligible residents must be 18-years-old, an Oakland resident and a U.S. resident or green card holder.
The program, which puts free cash in the hands of voters to spend on campaigns, launches in 2026.
Sponsored message
A group called Los Angeles for Democracy Vouchers is lobbying L.A. to institute democracy vouchers.
Previous efforts have failed
Lange said two other efforts to overturn the statewide ban on public financing failed in 2006 and 2010.
That was before the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2010 landmark Citizens United decision, which prohibited restrictions on expenditures in politics.
“That decision really, really exploded the amount of money spent in politics and really raised the understanding that voters have about the problems of big money in politics,” Lange said.
Opponents of public financing of elections argue it diverts public money from more pressing needs. Republicans have generally opposed using taxpayer dollars to finance political campaigns.
“People when they pay taxes want to pay for schools, fire departments, libraries, roads, that sort of thing,” David Kline of the California Taxpayers Association said. “The last thing they want to pay for is a negative political ad that is going to hit them on the radio or T.V. during election season.”
Sponsored message
He noted someone you disagree with is going to end up getting your tax dollars under public financing of campaigns.
UCLA Law Professor Rick Hasen, director of the school’s Safeguarding Democracy Project, called public financing of elections “potentially democratizing.”
“Some of the systems have allowed for more non-traditional candidates to run - more women and racial minorities for example,” he said.
But some worry that empowering small dollar donors with matching funds can fuel more extreme candidates, Hasen said, noting those candidates can attract large numbers of small donors.
“If you give matching funds, you might be fueling that tendency to reward flashier or more extreme candidates,” he said.
Hasen noted public financing does nothing to prevent exorbitant spending by outside groups like labor unions, corporations and wealthy individuals on campaigns.
Nonetheless, Dora Rose, of the League of Women Voters, said public financing has been a top priority of the organization.
“Public financing really helps engage unrepresented communities in the political process and it makes our democracy ultimately much stronger,” she said.
Incumbents may balk
It's far from clear that the Democrat dominated state Legislature will place the measure on the ballot.
Politicians elected under one system tend to like that system, said Fredric Woocher, an attorney and recognized expert on campaign finance law.
“Obviously, under the current system it's easier to raise funds as an incumbent than it is as a challenger,” he told LAist.
Woocher said, progressive candidates in Los Angeles who otherwise may have been underfunded have benefitted from public financing.
“We’ve seen a number of these progressive candidates compete in elections and win in races where they probably wouldn’t have been able to without public financing,” he said.
Woocher pointed to the victory of progressive candidate Zohran Mamdani in New York’s Democratic primary for mayor as another example of matching funds helping a progressive candidate.
Umberg, one of the sponsors of the bill, said if the Legislature places the measure on the ballot and voters approve it, voters in individual cities would still need to approve public financing. “Its not mandatory,” he said.
“The playing field is never going to be completely level but it is a step toward leveling the playing field where the average Joe or Jane has a more profound voice than they do today,” Umberg said.
The bill is currently being held in the Assembly Appropriations Committee. A vote is expected on Aug. 29.
If approved, it would move to the full Assembly.

## Should state and local governments have the option to provide public funding for election campaigns?
The measure would allow any state or local government to set up a public financing program for election campaigns.
Candidates would need to meet certain eligibility criteria and agree to spending limits.
The funds could not be used for legal defense costs, fines or repayment of personal loans.
Proposition 4 would repeal a 1988 ban on using taxpayer dollars for election campaigns.
Currently, only charter cities and counties can bypass that ban.

A group of legislators is seeking to lift the ban on public financing for elections in California, a move to counter the ever-increasing amount of money spent on campaigns in the Golden State.
Supporters say the California Fair Elections Act could be a game changer for underfunded candidates facing well-financed opponents and make races more competitive.
“The California Fair Elections Act is all about trying to improve our Democracy and elections,” said Sen. Ben Allen (D-Santa Monica), who co-authored the bill, in a statement to LAist. “Public financing programs serve as a tool to lessen the power of big money, expand opportunities for more people to run for office, and allow candidates to focus more on voter appeal instead of donor appeal.”
If passed, SB42, would place the measure on the November 2026 ballot. Sen. Tom Umberg (D-Anaheim) and Sen. Sabrina Cervantes (D-Riverside) are sponsors.
Common Cause, a group that fights to strengthen democracy, is among the bill’s backers.
“It’s essentially leveling the playing field,” said Sean McMorris, the group’s transparency, ethics and accountability program manager. “It’s also an attempt to diversify the candidate field, which gives voters more choice.”
Opponents of the bill, including the California Taxpayers Association, say public money should not be given to people running for office — that the money is better spent on services for the public.
Sponsored message
Right now, only cities governed by their own charter may enact public financing. And five of the state's 121 charter cities, including Los Angeles, Long Beach, San Francisco, Oakland and Berkeley, have done that.
Under the proposed ballot measure, the state’s other 361 cities and 58 counties would be able to set up public financing in their jurisdictions. In addition, the state Legislature could establish public financing for statewide offices, the senate and the assembly.
The measure would allow a candidate to accept public funds unless the funds are earmarked by a state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety.
The bill would also require candidates to abide by expenditure limits and prohibit public funds from being used to pay legal defense fees, fines or to repay personal loans to their campaign.
Ways to publicly finance campaigns
There are a variety of public campaign financing schemes where governments use taxpayer money to fund candidates who agree to limit their spending.
In Los Angeles, candidates for City Council who agree to spending limits must first raise $5 each from 100 residents in their respective districts and about $77,000 from residents anywhere in the city before they qualify for matching funds.
Sponsored message
In the last election cycle, the maximum matching funds for the primary and general elections combined was $425,000. The city doled out $3.8 million in matching funds.
Trent Lange of the California Clean Money Campaign, which backs the bill, said public financing has helped diversify the L.A. City Council, which has gone from one woman member a decade ago to eight now.
“All of them were elected using public funds that helped them get their message out and run and compete,” Lange told LAist.
In the 2022 L.A. mayor’s race, billionaire Rick Caruso spent more than $100 million compared to Mayor Karen Bass’ roughly $10 million. But Bass benefitted from $2.3 million in matching funds.
Caruso rejected spending limits, which prohibited him from receiving matching funds.
In Oakland, voters have approved a voucher program. Under the program, the city will disperse $100 in so-called Democracy Dollar vouchers to eligible residents who can then give the money to the candidate of their choice. Eligible residents must be 18-years-old, an Oakland resident and a U.S. resident or green card holder.
The program, which puts free cash in the hands of voters to spend on campaigns, launches in 2026.
Sponsored message
A group called Los Angeles for Democracy Vouchers is lobbying L.A. to institute democracy vouchers.
Previous efforts have failed
Lange said two other efforts to overturn the statewide ban on public financing failed in 2006 and 2010.
That was before the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2010 landmark Citizens United decision, which prohibited restrictions on expenditures in politics.
“That decision really, really exploded the amount of money spent in politics and really raised the understanding that voters have about the problems of big money in politics,” Lange said.
Opponents of public financing of elections argue it diverts public money from more pressing needs. Republicans have generally opposed using taxpayer dollars to finance political campaigns.
“People when they pay taxes want to pay for schools, fire departments, libraries, roads, that sort of thing,” David Kline of the California Taxpayers Association said. “The last thing they want to pay for is a negative political ad that is going to hit them on the radio or T.V. during election season.”
Sponsored message
He noted someone you disagree with is going to end up getting your tax dollars under public financing of campaigns.
UCLA Law Professor Rick Hasen, director of the school’s Safeguarding Democracy Project, called public financing of elections “potentially democratizing.”
“Some of the systems have allowed for more non-traditional candidates to run - more women and racial minorities for example,” he said.
But some worry that empowering small dollar donors with matching funds can fuel more extreme candidates, Hasen said, noting those candidates can attract large numbers of small donors.
“If you give matching funds, you might be fueling that tendency to reward flashier or more extreme candidates,” he said.
Hasen noted public financing does nothing to prevent exorbitant spending by outside groups like labor unions, corporations and wealthy individuals on campaigns.
Nonetheless, Dora Rose, of the League of Women Voters, said public financing has been a top priority of the organization.
“Public financing really helps engage unrepresented communities in the political process and it makes our democracy ultimately much stronger,” she said.
Incumbents may balk
It's far from clear that the Democrat dominated state Legislature will place the measure on the ballot.
Politicians elected under one system tend to like that system, said Fredric Woocher, an attorney and recognized expert on campaign finance law.
“Obviously, under the current system it's easier to raise funds as an incumbent than it is as a challenger,” he told LAist.
Woocher said, progressive candidates in Los Angeles who otherwise may have been underfunded have benefitted from public financing.
“We’ve seen a number of these progressive candidates compete in elections and win in races where they probably wouldn’t have been able to without public financing,” he said.
Woocher pointed to the victory of progressive candidate Zohran Mamdani in New York’s Democratic primary for mayor as another example of matching funds helping a progressive candidate.
Umberg, one of the sponsors of the bill, said if the Legislature places the measure on the ballot and voters approve it, voters in individual cities would still need to approve public financing. “Its not mandatory,” he said.
“The playing field is never going to be completely level but it is a step toward leveling the playing field where the average Joe or Jane has a more profound voice than they do today,” Umberg said.
The bill is currently being held in the Assembly Appropriations Committee. A vote is expected on Aug. 29.
If approved, it would move to the full Assembly.

Now let me look at the empirical evidence on public campaign financing effectiveness — this is the crux of the "is it better" question. Key studies:
- NYC matching funds program: research by Michael Malbin, Donald Green, Peter Frascino — increased small-donor participation, diversified donor pool.
- Seattle democracy vouchers: study by Barber, Hill, Legace — 2022 JPubE study found vouchers increased number of candidates by 86%? Actually the study found increased candidate pool and more diverse donors.
- Maine/Arizona: studies finding increased competition (Donovan et al.), GAO finding no effect.
- Hall & Rogers / "The Impact of Public Financing on Electoral Competition" (Stanford) — found AZ/ME increased competition.
- Also concerns: matching funds may advantage more extreme candidates (Hasen).

Also important consideration: Prop 4 is permissive — it doesn't itself spend money. It removes a state-law ban so local governments can decide. The fiscal cost of a yes vote directly is trivially small (few hundred thousand dollars/year for FPPC guidance). The downside risk is future local decisions, which local voters can then influence. The upside is enabling a policy tool used in 15 states + DC and 26+ localities.

Note there's an interesting nuance: a "no" vote preserves a statewide ban that voters enacted in 1988 (Prop 73). Note that Prop 73's public financing ban provision was actually held partially unconstitutional in Johnson v. Bradley (1992). Hmm.

Another consideration: The measure also triples fines for foreign money in elections — a genuine reform benefit unrelated to public financing. That's a plus.

Concerns raised by credible nonpartisan-ish sources (SF Chronicle): no requirement of independent oversight body for local programs; FPPC exempted; leaves design decisions to politicians who benefit; no evidence that existing CA programs work well.

Concerns raised by taxpayer groups: no cap on amount, no limit on number of candidates, candidates could also take special interest money.

Let me verify some factual claims:
1. "Prop 4 allows public financing of candidates for county political party committees" — is that true? The Political Reform Act's definition of "candidate" (Gov Code 82011) is "an individual who is seeking elective office" — I think that includes county central committee. Let me check.
2. "Candidates don't even have to qualify for the ballot to get taxpayer money" — Prop 4 prohibits "strict criteria" from including signature requirements. That's true: 'Strict criteria' shall not include requirements that candidates receive a specified number of signatures... So a program couldn't require petition signatures. But local governments could still impose other requirements. Hmm, actually this is a substantive criticism: normally you'd require ballot qualification. But the drafters excluded signature requirements to make it easier for under-resourced candidates. It does create a risk of funding non-viable candidates — though "broad-based support" via small-dollar contributions is a filter, and expenditure limits + voluntary participation reduce risk.

Actually wait — is the ban on signature requirements really about that? Let me think. In California, some local programs require candidates to gather signatures to qualify for the ballot AND additional requirements for public financing. The Prop 4 language limits the "strict criteria" to small-dollar contributions/vouchers and prohibits requiring signatures or a total dollar amount above $10/contributor. That's aimed at avoiding wealth-based qualification thresholds. It's a design choice, arguably reasonable but with a risk.

3. Note the important point: even after Prop 4, local public financing programs would still generally require voter approval if funded by a new tax (Prop 13/218/26). But if funded from existing general fund, a city council could approve it by ordinance without voter approval. Umberg said "voters in individual cities would still need to approve public financing" — actually not necessarily; a city council can adopt an ordinance. That's a legitimate concern: it enables politicians to vote themselves taxpayer money without direct voter approval. But: (a) local voters can vote them out; (b) many cities require voter approval for new taxes; (c) charter cities already do this.

Let me check some more evidence: NYC's program effects; Seattle democracy voucher effects; also cost per resident figures. And check the "26 localities / 14 states" claim.

Also let me check what Reform California and the CA Republican Party say, and whether there's any notable Democrat opposition.

Let me also check the Mercury News pro op-ed and Dan Schnur's op-ed piece.

Let me do a couple more searches.

Proposition 4 would repeal the Political Reform Act's ban on using public money for political candidates' campaigns.

During each election cycle, the city of Seattle distributes four $25 vouchers to every registered voter, which may be donated to and redeemed by campaigns for city office.
Through a difference-in-differences research design, we study the causal effect of Seattle’s program on various outcomes in city council elections in the first two cycles after implementation, with comparison cities drawn from large cities in Washington and California.

We further estimate a highly significant 86% increase in number of candidates coupled with substantial decreases in incumbent electoral success.

## Abstract
Seattle's Democracy Vouchers program provides a unique form of public financing for political campaigns in which voters decide how to allocate public funding across candidates.
This paper is the first to study the effects of public financing for political campaigns on political participation.
I estimate that the Democracy Vouchers program increases voter turnout by 4.9 percentage points, suggesting that public financing programs can increase political participation.
I also find that campaigns become more reliant on small contributions.
For city council candidates, dollars from small contributions under $100 increase by 156% while dollars from large contributions over $250 decrease by 93%.

The Effects of Public Campaign Funding: Evidence from Seattle's Democracy Voucher Program, 2022.
Journal of Public Economics 211:104666 (with Thomas Noonen)
During each election cycle, the city of Seattle distributes four $25 vouchers to every registered voter, which may be donated to and redeemed by campaigns for city office.
Through a difference-in-differences research design, we study the causal effect of Seattle's program on various outcomes in city council elections in the first two cycles after implementation, with comparison cities drawn from large cities in Washington and California.
We find a 53% increase in total contributions and a 350% increase in number of unique donors; these effects are largely explained by large increases in small donations, defined as contributions less than $200.
We find statistically insignificant evidence of decreases in private donations, although our point estimates suggest moderate-to-substantial crowd-out ratios.
We further estimate a highly significant 86\% increase in number of candidates coupled with substantial decreases in incumbent electoral success.
These results provide some of the first causal evidence of the effect of decentralized public campaign finance schemes, while speaking to the impacts of campaign regulation more generally on donation activity, candidate entry, and incumbency advantage.

Seattle's Democracy Vouchers program provides a unique form of public financing for political campaigns in which voters decide how to allocate public funding across candidates.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
Good. Now I have strong evidence that well-designed public financing programs (Seattle vouchers, NYC matching) measurably increase donor diversity, candidate entry, reduce incumbency advantage, and increase turnout. But design matters (LA's program was much less effective than NYC's). Oakland's older program showed no evidence of reducing wealthy donor influence but increased competition. GAO found no effect on candidate numbers in AZ/ME.

Now let me examine the counterarguments more carefully and check for any additional facts:

1. Does Prop 4 require local voter approval before a city creates a program? No — city councils could adopt by ordinance. That's a genuine accountability concern. However, note: if a new tax is needed, Prop 13/218 requires voter approval in most cases. And local officials are accountable via elections. Also, note that the LA Public Press article says: "the measure would authorize the state legislature or local government agencies to enact public funding programs for campaigns without the need for voter approval." That's a real risk.

2. Cost. If widely adopted, costs could be significant. LA's program cost $3.8M matching funds in one cycle. NYC's program cost ~$30M+ in 2021 (actually $210M+? Let's check: NYC 2021 public funds payments were about $210 million? Hmm — NYC's 2021 program paid out ~$200 million? Let me verify. Actually, in 2021 NYC's matching funds program paid out approximately $210 million? I recall the 2021 CFB program paid $203 million. Let me check quickly. Not essential.)

3. The "no limit on the number of candidates" claim — technically true, the measure doesn't cap number; local programs set thresholds.

4. The "no limit on how much" claim — the measure requires expenditure limits (voluntary) be set by each jurisdiction, but doesn't set a ceiling. True.

5. The claim candidates could get public money and still take special interest money — true; the measure doesn't prohibit participants from also raising private money up to contribution limits. Though participants must accept spending caps.

6. "Candidates don't even have to qualify for the ballot" — the measure prohibits using signature requirements as part of strict criteria. But jurisdictions could require other things? The definition says "strict criteria" means the requirements set by statute/ordinance/charter that candidates must meet to receive public funds. These criteria SHALL require candidates to demonstrate broad-based support in their district, such as by requiring candidates to receive small-dollar contributions or vouchers from a specified number of voting-age residents. And (C) says strict criteria shall not include requirements that candidates receive a specified number of signatures or raise a specified total dollar amount of more than $10 per contributor. So a jurisdiction could require e.g. $5 from 500 residents. That's a real threshold. So the "blank check" claim is overblown — there must be a broad-based support threshold. But it's true there's no requirement of ballot qualification.

7. FPPC not responsible for administration/enforcement of local programs — true, and the Chronicle's point about lack of mandated local oversight is legitimate. But note: FPPC would still enforce the Political Reform Act generally (disclosure, contribution limits). And local programs would need some administering body. Also existing local programs are administered by city clerks/ethics commissions.

8. Triples foreign-money fines: good provision.

Let me also consider: what's the actual expected fiscal impact? LAO says: minor state costs (few hundred thousand per year) for FPPC guidance. Costs of any programs depend on future decisions.

Now, how to decide? The question asks: "Is it better to vote yes or no on this prop?" I need to come to a decision and answer with only "yes" or "no".

Let me weigh:

Arguments for YES:
- California is uniquely the only state banning local public financing; it's a legacy of Prop 73 (1988), which had its own legal troubles and was upheld in part. The ban strips local self-determination.
- Prop 4 is permissive, not mandatory: it spends no money itself; direct fiscal cost is negligible. Local communities and the state can choose.
- Strong empirical evidence that well-designed programs (NYC 6:1/8:1 match, Seattle vouchers) broaden the donor base, increase candidate entry, reduce incumbent advantage, increase turnout, and elect more women and people of color.
- Money in CA politics has exploded (Steyer $213M; Building a Better California ~$300M; $1B+ in state candidate races since 2020). After Citizens United, you can't restrict independent spending — public financing is one of the few constitutionally permissible tools to counterbalance.
- Includes taxpayer safeguards: no education/transportation/public safety funds; expenditure limits required; broad-based support thresholds; no legal defense/fines/personal loan repayment; anti-discrimination by party/incumbency; triples foreign-money fines.
- Broad coalition support: LWV, Common Cause, ACLU California Action, CNA, CalFed of Teachers, CA Democratic Party, Consumer Watchdog, SPUR, Sacramento Bee/McClatchy boards, LA Times (George Skelton at least; and the golden-state.org op-ed).
- Voting no preserves a status quo that entrenches incumbency advantage and big-donor dependence.

Arguments for NO:
- No cap on program size or number of candidates; details left to politicians who benefit directly (self-dealing risk).
- No requirement of independent oversight; FPPC explicitly exempted from local program administration/enforcement.
- No requirement of local voter approval — a city council could vote itself taxpayer money.
- Evidence of effectiveness is mixed; CA's own charter-city programs haven't been rigorously evaluated; Oakland 2013 study found no reduction in wealthy-donor influence; GAO found no candidate-entry effect in AZ/ME.
- Budget context: state and local governments face deficits; new discretionary spending categories risk crowding out services.
- Voters have rejected similar measures 3 times (2000, 2006, 2010); current polling shows majority opposed.
- Candidates can still take special-interest money, so it doesn't remove big money — it just adds another stream (more total money in politics, possibly more ads).

Hmm. Which is "better"?

I think a reasonable, well-researched judgment: The measure is fundamentally about restoring local option and permitting a policy tool with credible evidence of benefits, with real (if modest) safeguards, at essentially zero immediate fiscal cost. The strongest "no" arguments come from ideologically anti-tax groups and rely on exaggerations ("blank check," "no limits") that the text contradicts (expenditure limits are mandatory for participants; broad-based support criteria are mandatory; education/transportation/public safety funds are carved out; no legal defense/fines/personal loans). The Chronicle's concern about oversight is legitimate but is a design detail that local governments adopting programs would have to address, and the FPPC exemption largely reflects that the FPPC has no staff capacity to run 400+ local programs — SF and LA run theirs through local ethics commissions.

The risk asymmetry: voting NO permanently forecloses an option for every jurisdiction in California (including future state-level programs) and preserves a status quo where billionaires and corporations dominate. Voting YES creates an option that still requires a further, visible political decision at the state or local level — a decision voters can then contest and reverse. YES is the lower-regret, higher-option-value choice, with negligible immediate fiscal impact.

Also note: polling shows the measure trailing, but that doesn't tell us what's "better."

I'll answer yes.

Actually, let me double-check a couple more things to be thorough — the Reform California position, and whether there's any hidden provision (e.g., does Prop 4 also allow public financing for ballot measures? No — it's limited to candidates). And check the "county political party committee" claim. Let me quickly verify Gov Code 82011 definition of candidate.

Let me also check the KQED voter guide "No Argument" and the IGS endorsement table to see balance. And check the Golden State op-ed (LA Times editorial board? golden-state.org appears to be a group). Let me do one more round.
